question:
Patient note:
An 85-year-old male retiree who has lived in an assisted-living apartment for the past four years was delivered to the medical intensive care holding alcove thirty minutes after staff noticed that he was breathing faster than usual and running a fever; the facility nurse reported that over the preceding week he had taken only half of his meals and had skipped his customary afternoon walks because of progressive fatigue and a “raspy” cough. His past history is notable for longstanding seropositive rheumatoid arthritis managed with low-dose oral prednisone since his late sixties and with weekly methotrexate until six months ago, as well as well-controlled type 2 diabetes treated by diet alone; he has never been intubated, dialyzed, transplanted, or subjected to a recent operation, and no plans for elective or emergent surgery had been made for this admission. According to the transport sheet, paramedics found him sitting in a high-back chair, able to speak in full sentences yet mildly confused about the calendar; fingertip oximetry on ambient air displayed 86 %, so they applied a Venturi device delivering precisely 44 % inspired oxygen, but gave no intravenous fluids, antimicrobial agents, bronchodilators, vasopressors, analgesics, or antipyretics during the fifteen-minute ride. Upon stretcher arrival—and before any emergency department therapy—the first full set of vital signs recorded an oral temperature of 101.2 °F, a regular heart rate of 87 beats per minute confirmed on three-lead telemetry, an observed respiratory rate of 22 breaths per minute with mild intercostal retractions, and a non-invasive blood pressure of 119/69 mm Hg that was reproducible on the contralateral arm. The patient opened his eyes when addressed by name, gave appropriate words though he believed the month to be February instead of April, and obeyed two-step commands, yielding a Glasgow Coma Score of 14 without sedatives, ethanol, or narcotics in his system. He was thin, slightly diaphoretic, and flushed; capillary refill was less than two seconds, and there was no peripheral cyanosis or dependent edema. Jugular venous pulsations were not distended at 30 degrees. Cardiac examination disclosed a crisp S1 and single S2 without murmurs, rubs, or gallops; distal pulses were 2+ and symmetric. Pulmonary auscultation revealed coarse crackles over the right lower posterior field and faint bronchial breath sounds in that region, while percussion there was duller than the left. The abdomen was soft, nondistended, and nontender, with active bowel sounds; no organomegaly or flank discomfort was elicited. Extremities displayed no digital clubbing or petechiae, and there were no focal motor or sensory deficits on a brief neurologic survey. Nine minutes after arrival, a right radial arterial sample drawn while he remained on 44 % oxygen produced the following immediate blood-gas values: pH 7.43, PaCO₂ 35 mm Hg, and PaO₂ 53 mm Hg; end-tidal capnography showed 34 mm Hg, consistent with adequate alveolar ventilation despite significant hypoxemia. Simultaneously obtained serum chemistry revealed sodium 138 mmol/L, potassium 4.0 mmol/L, chloride 101 mmol/L, bicarbonate 25 mmol/L, glucose 118 mg/dL, blood urea nitrogen 19 mg/dL, and creatinine 1.1 mg/dL, essentially matching his baseline of 1.0 mg/dL documented at an outpatient visit two months prior and indicating preserved renal function without acute or chronic failure. Complete blood count returned a white-cell count of 14 250 cells/mm³ with 82 % segmented neutrophils, hematocrit 37 %, hemoglobin 12.3 g/dL, and platelets 212 000 /µL. Point-of-care lactate measured 2.2 mmol/L. A portable anteroposterior chest radiograph obtained before any pharmacologic intervention showed a dense consolidation occupying the right lower lobe with air-bronchograms and no pleural effusion; cardiac silhouette and mediastinal contours were normal for age. Focused cardiac ultrasound demonstrated a small but vigorously contracting left ventricle, no regional wall-motion abnormality, and an inferior vena cava that collapsed more than 50 % with quiet inspiration, suggesting relative euvolemia. Bedside lung ultrasound corroborated the radiographic finding, displaying focal B-lines and tissue-like echotexture in the right posterobasal zone. Electrocardiography printed during the arterial puncture exhibited normal sinus rhythm at 86 beats per minute, PR 160 ms, QRS 94 ms, QTc 430 ms, and no acute ischemic changes. A Foley catheter placed purely for monitoring produced 80 mL of clear yellow urine in the first quarter hour, indicating adequate perfusion. Crucially, during the forty-minute interval from discovery at the facility through transfer and initial ICU evaluation, the patient had not yet received antibiotics, glucocorticoid stress dosing, intravenous crystalloids, vasopressors, diuretics, or antipyretics, so the recorded physiologic and laboratory values—temperature 101.2 °F, systolic pressure 119 mm Hg, diastolic pressure 69 mm Hg, pulse 87 beats per minute, respirations 22 per minute, arterial pH 7.43, serum sodium 138 mmol/L, serum potassium 4.0 mmol/L, creatinine 1.1 mg/dL, hematocrit 37 %, white blood cell count 14 250 /mm³, fraction of inspired oxygen 44 %, and arterial oxygen tension 53 mm Hg—faithfully depict his untreated presentation for community-acquired pneumonia complicated by hypoxemic respiratory failure in the context of chronic corticosteroid exposure.

Question: What is the patient's APACHE II score?
solution:
APACHE II sums acute physiology, age, and chronic health points. Use the supplied admission measurements.
1. Vital signs: Temperature 101.2 °F ≈ 38.4 °C → 0. Mean arterial pressure = (119 + 2 × 69)/3 ≈ 86 mm Hg → 0. Heart rate 87/min → 0; respiratory rate 22/min → 0.
2. Oxygenation and acid–base status: FiO₂ is 0.44 (<0.50), so score PaO₂ rather than the alveolar–arterial gradient. PaO₂ 53 mm Hg is <55 → 4. Arterial pH 7.43 → 0.
3. Other laboratory values: Sodium 138 mmol/L → 0; potassium 4.0 mmol/L → 0; creatinine 1.1 mg/dL → 0; hematocrit 37% → 0; WBC 14.25 × 10³/µL → 0.
4. Neurologic points = 15 − recorded GCS = 15 − 14 = 1. Acute physiology subtotal = 4 + 1 = 5.
5. Age 85 (≥75 years) → 6. Counting longstanding systemic prednisone therapy as chronic immunosuppression, this nonoperative admission adds 5 chronic health points.
Total = 5 + 6 + 5 = 16.
Final answer: 16
